name: Argentina
summary_text: Argentina's Gender Identity Law 26,743, promulgated on 24 May 2012 after approval in the Chamber of Deputies and in the Senate on 9 May 2012, allows adults to change legal gender, image and birth name on civil registries without surgery, hormone therapy, a psychiatric diagnosis of abnormality, or approval by a doctor or judge. The United Nations described the statute as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.  On 20 July 2021, Decree 476/2021 required the national civil registry to offer a third gender marker X on all national identity cards and passports, including for non-citizen permanent residents holding Argentine identity cards. Mendoza Province and Santa Fe Province had earlier allowed applicants to leave the sex entry blank.  The same 2012 law grants adults access to sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy through public and private health care plans, with equal access stated for non-binary, transgender and gender non-conforming persons.  In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for persons under age 18. Legal experts described the measure as illegal and unconstitutional and as a setback for adolescents' rights. In April 2025 a Federal Court ruled the ban unconstitutional, restoring access nationwide.  A second February 2025 decree governs the housing of transgender people in prisons. The sources do not provide its operative terms.  Consensual same-sex sexual activity has been lawful since 1887 under Law No. 1,920. Same-sex marriage was legalized on 15 July 2010 with the same benefits and protections as opposite-sex marriage, including adoption since July 2010. A nationwide registered partnership, the union convivencial under the Civil and Commercial Code, has been available since 1 August 2015.  Penal Code Article 80(4), as amended in 2012, imposes life imprisonment for homicide motivated by hatred based on gender identity or expression and on sexual orientation. As of 2019 no national law expressly addressed discrimination or harassment based on gender identity. Outright International records that anti-discrimination protections exist through national and provincial laws. The national anti-discrimination agency was abolished and shut down in February 2024 as a public-spending measure.  The Observatorio Nacional de Crimenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours. The monitoring group described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina.  In interviews in Buenos Aires on 4 April 2025, reported on 10 April 2025, trans activists including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayan and for Lohana Berkins said the policies of the Milei administration had made the community more vulnerable to violence. Sacayan, a trans activist, was killed in 2015.  On 5 April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of Diana Sacayan. The Court rejected attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that a cassation court had removed in 2020, with the result that the gender-motivated-crime aggravator is currently not applied in the case.  Outright International's Argentina overview, updated 12 March 2026, notes that Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalize marriage equality and that its 2012 law allowed legal gender change without medical procedures or judicial approval. Its current assessment records negative evaluations on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration.

name: American Samoa
summary_text: American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.  Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applicants. The policy is challenged in federal courts, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs; trans and nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, with some stranded abroad.  Same-sex marriage remains formally contested in the territory. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it. In 2015 American Samoa was the only United States territory whose attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands moved to apply it. In January 2016 a district court judge confirmed by the Senate told legislators he had not read Obergefell and that the district court did not deal with the ruling. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date; the litigation path runs through the High Court of American Samoa against the Territorial Registrar, then the United States Department of the Interior. As of mid-2024 the local ban was still treated on-island as operative, with its constitutional durability an open question under academic study.  Trans-specific violence and protection machinery are documented. In September 2023 the United States Justice Department settled an employment-discrimination case against the American Samoa Government over harassment of a transgender employee; a June 2023 federal civil action cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity; and in February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.  Local cultural context shapes daily expectations. The Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa, formed in 2010, frames fa'afafine as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture; reserved public behaviour is expected of people of all orientations, and homosexuality is widely accepted within Samoan culture compared with neighbouring Pacific states.
